title: Propositional logic
objective: Identify propositions, evaluate connectives and truth tables, and apply logical equivalences.

blocks.text: Statements with truth values

Logic studies correct reasoning. A proposition is a declarative statement with a definite truth value: true or false. A false statement such as 10 < 4 is still a proposition. Commands and questions are not propositions. A simple proposition states one basic claim; a compound proposition combines claims using logical connectives. Logic supports programming conditions, digital circuits, database queries and software verification.
Connectives

Negation ¬p reverses the truth value of p. Conjunction p ∧ q is true only when both inputs are true. Inclusive disjunction p ∨ q is true when either input or both inputs are true. A conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false. A biconditional p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value. These are truth-functional definitions; an ordinary-language causal relationship should not be inferred from a material implication alone.
Truth tables and classifications

A truth table considers every assignment of truth values. There are 2^n assignments for n distinct propositions: four rows for two propositions and eight for three. A tautology is true on every row, a contradiction is false on every row, and a contingency is true on some rows and false on others. Thus p ∨ ¬p is a tautology, p ∧ ¬p is a contradiction, and p itself is contingent.
Equivalence laws

Logical equivalence means that two expressions agree on every truth-table row. Double negation gives ¬¬p ≡ p. De Morgan’s laws are ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. The identity laws are p ∧ T ≡ p and p ∨ F ≡ p. The domination laws are p ∨ T ≡ T and p ∧ F ≡ F.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: Let p be true and q false. Then ¬p is false, p ∧ q is false, p ∨ q is true, p → q is false, and p ↔ q is false. To check ¬p ∨ q, first negate p, obtaining false, and then evaluate false OR false: false. This agrees with p → q on that row.

blocks.title: Avoid this mistake
blocks.text: Do not treat OR as exclusive unless stated. An implication with a false antecedent is true in its truth table; it does not establish a real-world cause.
What to remember

10 is less than 4.. A false declarative statement still has a definite truth value. When both p and q are true. Conjunction requires both components to be true. T. Inclusive disjunction needs at least one true component.

title: Predicate logic
objective: Evaluate predicates over a stated domain and translate or negate quantified statements.

blocks.text: Predicates and substitution

A predicate contains one or more variables. The open statement P(x): x > 5 does not yet assert a definite proposition until x is assigned or quantified over a specified domain. Substitution makes P(8) true and P(3) false. The domain of discourse states which values are being considered and can change whether a quantified claim is true.
Universal and existential claims

The universal quantifier ∀ means for every element in the domain. The existential quantifier ∃ means for at least one element. For D = {2, 6, 9} and P(x): x > 5, ∀x P(x) is false because 2 is a counterexample, while ∃x P(x) is true because 6 and 9 are witnesses. One witness proves an existential claim; a universal claim must hold throughout the domain.
Negation

Negating a quantified statement switches its quantifier and negates its predicate: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Therefore not all students passed means that at least one student did not pass. It does not say that nobody passed. Nobody passed means every student failed to pass, not merely that one failed.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: Let S(x) mean x submitted the assignment, with the domain restricted to students in the class. The statement not all students submitted becomes ¬∀x S(x), equivalent to ∃x ¬S(x). A single student who did not submit is a witness to the negated universal claim.

blocks.text: Always specify the domain. Do not turn not everyone into no one; those claims have different strengths.

True. Substitute 8: 8 > 5 is true. False. 3 is not greater than 5. For every element. The universal quantifier ranges over all members of the stated domain.

title: Sets and set operations
objective: Recognise sets and subsets, evaluate set operations, and use inclusion-exclusion.

blocks.text: Elements and kinds of sets

A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. Writing 2 ∈ A means 2 belongs to A; 2 ∉ A means it does not. Repeating an element does not create another distinct member. The empty set ∅ has no elements, a singleton has one, a finite set has a finite number, and an infinite set has infinitely many. The lecture uses N = {1, 2, 3, ...} for the natural numbers.
Subsets and operations

A ⊆ B means every member of A is also a member of B. The union A ∪ B contains members of either set, including their overlap. The intersection A ∩ B contains only shared members. A − B contains members of A that do not belong to B, so direction matters. Relative to a universal set U, the complement Aᶜ is U − A. A universal set must be specified before a complement is calculated.
Counting without double-counting

For two finite sets, |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. Adding the two set sizes counts each shared element twice, so the intersection is subtracted once. If 30 students know Java, 25 know Python and 10 know both, 45 know at least one language. Exactly 20 know only Java and 15 know only Python. This information alone does not determine how many know neither language because the class size was not given.

blocks.title: Work through an example

blocks.title: Avoid this mistake
blocks.text: Union includes the overlap; difference is directional; a complement depends on its universal set.
What to remember

A well-defined collection of distinct objects. A set is defined by membership and contains distinct elements. 1. A singleton has exactly one element. Every member of A belongs to B. The subset condition checks every member of A against B.

title: Functions
objective: Distinguish domain and codomain, test the function condition, and recognise injective, surjective and bijective mappings.

blocks.text: A mapping with one output per input

A mathematical function f: A → B assigns exactly one element of B to every element of A. A is its domain and B is its codomain. Every domain element needs an output, and one input cannot be assigned two different outputs. Two different inputs may share one output and still define a function. The range consists of the outputs actually attained and can be a proper subset of the codomain.
Injective, surjective and bijective

A one-to-one or injective function sends distinct inputs to distinct outputs. An onto or surjective function reaches every member of its codomain. A bijection has both properties: each codomain element has exactly one preimage, so its inverse maps the codomain back to the domain as a function. Surjectivity cannot be judged from a formula without specifying the codomain.
A computing connection

A grade calculation takes a score as input and returns a grade. Such a mapping can be many-to-one, since several scores may receive the same grade. It is still a function if every allowed score receives exactly one grade. Programming routines are related to this idea, but can have side effects; the mathematical definition is the one used for these exercises.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: Let A = {1, 2}, B = {a, b}, and f(1) = a, f(2) = b. The mapping is a function because each input has one output. It is injective because the outputs differ and surjective because both a and b are reached. Therefore it is bijective, with f⁻¹(a) = 1 and f⁻¹(b) = 2.

blocks.title: Avoid this mistake
blocks.text: Many-to-one mappings can be functions. Reaching every value in the range is automatic; being onto requires reaching every value in the stated codomain.
What to remember

The domain. A contains the allowed inputs. The codomain. The codomain contains the permitted outputs, whether or not all are reached. It has exactly one output. The function condition requires existence and uniqueness of each input’s image.

title: Sequences and summation
objective: Find terms of arithmetic and geometric sequences and evaluate finite sums.

blocks.text: Ordered terms

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. Its nth term aₙ specifies the value at position n. In these notes positions begin at n = 1, so aₙ = 2n gives 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ... . The order of terms matters, unlike ordinary set membership.
Arithmetic sequences

An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference d between consecutive terms. Its nth term is aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d. In 3, 7, 11, 15, ... , the first term is 3 and d = 4. The fifth term is 3 + (5 − 1) × 4 = 19. Using n instead of n − 1 counts one extra step from the first term.
Geometric sequences

A geometric sequence has a constant ratio r between consecutive terms. Its nth term is aₙ = a₁r^(n − 1). In 2, 6, 18, 54, ... , a₁ = 2 and r = 3. The fifth term is 2 × 3^4 = 162. To distinguish the two sequence types, compare successive differences and successive ratios instead of assuming a pattern from one pair.
Sigma notation

The symbol Σ means summation. In Σ from i = 1 to 5 of i, the index takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the terms are added, giving 15. The formula 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2 applies to the first n positive integers. A term formula finds one term; a summation adds several terms. They answer different questions.

blocks.title: Avoid this mistake
blocks.text: Use n − 1 in the nth-term formulas when indexing starts at 1. Do not confuse a term with the sum of terms.
What to remember
Its entries are ordered. A sequence assigns an order or index to its terms. 10. Substitute n = 5: 2 × 5 = 10. 4. Each term increases by 4.

title: Seventh-day Adventist philosophy of education
objective: Explain the chapter’s main ideas, distinguish its key terms, and apply them to an educational example.

blocks.text: Purpose and foundations

In the supplied chapter, Seventh-day Adventist education is Christ-centred and has a redemptive purpose: leading people toward God and restoring the image of God in human life. Education and redemption are described as closely united. The chapter locates the tradition’s historical roots in the Millerite movement and the Great Disappointment of 1844, and identifies biblical principles and Ellen G. White’s writings as central educational influences.
Knowledge and integration

The chapter presents Scripture and divine revelation as foundational sources of knowledge. Biblical integration means interpreting learning through this worldview across subjects, rather than merely adding a Bible class to an otherwise separate curriculum. The unity of truth is the belief that truth ultimately has one divine source. These statements describe the Adventist perspective taught by the handout, not a premise every philosophical school shares.
Whole-person development and service

Education addresses spiritual, intellectual, physical, emotional, moral, social and practical development. The chapter links healthful living and useful work with education, and emphasises community service as an expression of faith. Learning is intended to produce independent thinkers rather than passive reflectors of a teacher’s opinions. Parents, pastors and teachers share responsibility. The stated horizon includes service in this life and the life to come.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: A class studies a community problem, evaluates possible responses, carries out a service project and reflects on its ethical purpose. Intellectual inquiry, practical action, social responsibility and spiritual reflection work together instead of being treated as unrelated activities.

blocks.title: Avoid this mistake
blocks.text: Christ-centred education does not mean memorisation without thought. Do not repeat the handout’s undated school-count figures as current statistics.

title: The strength of wholistic education
objective: Explain the chapter’s main ideas, distinguish its key terms, and apply them to an educational example.

blocks.text: Head, heart and hand

Wholistic education develops the whole person. The chapter uses head, heart and hand to connect thought, character and practical competence. Head education cultivates mental faculties and thinking. Heart education concerns the convictions and values that guide thought and action. Hand education develops practical skills, manual work and useful service. None of the three substitutes for the others.
A lifelong and restorative purpose

Ellen G. White’s educational account concerns the whole being and the whole period of existence. Within this Christian framework, education seeks to restore the image of God and to direct body, mind and soul toward loving service. The chapter associates human development with increasing capacity, while interpreting the Fall as damaging human faculties and making restoration necessary.
Learning through responsibility

The chapter uses tending the Garden of Eden as an illustration of meaningful work, and refers to Moses’ Egyptian education as an example of broad preparation. Its educational lesson is that intellectual development should be joined with character and practical ability. Learners should become thoughtful agents who can respond responsibly to circumstances, rather than merely repeat what others think.

title: Christian curriculum design and instruction
objective: Explain the chapter’s main ideas, distinguish its key terms, and apply them to an educational example.

blocks.text: Curriculum as whole-person formation

The chapter describes Christian education as the harmonious development of physical, mental and spiritual powers. It treats God and Christ as the ultimate source of wisdom within its faith framework. Its curriculum illustrations connect intellectual learning with moral responsibility, practical activity and spiritual formation.
Educational settings in the handout

The Eden illustration presents God as teacher and nature as a lesson book, with obedience, tending the garden, naming creatures and studying creation as elements of learning. The Israelite model emphasises parents’ educational responsibility, instruction in God’s law and useful work. The Schools of the Prophets are associated with Samuel, Elijah and Elisha and with practical preparation as well as religious instruction.
Teaching and discernment

The Deuteronomy discussion says teachers should first internalise what they teach and then teach diligently. Diligence means sustained effort and commitment, not occasional instruction. Faith-and-learning integration depends on a teacher’s lived relationship with the beliefs being taught. Critical thinking involves reasoning, analysis, evaluation and the development of ideas; blind acceptance is not critical thinking. Discernment involves judging well. The handout’s FIRE acronym is Focus, Identify, Reframe, Exchange.

title: Truth and knowledge theories
objective: Explain the chapter’s main ideas, distinguish its key terms, and apply them to an educational example.

blocks.text: What epistemology asks

Epistemology studies the nature, sources and scope of knowledge. The chapter distinguishes practical know-how, sensory or empirical knowledge, reasoned understanding and intuitive insight. Rationalism emphasises reason and deduction; empiricism emphasises observation and experience. The scientific-method sequence in the notes is observation, hypothesis, experiment and analysis. Skeptical positions question whether particular knowledge claims, or knowledge more generally, can be justified.
Three accounts of truth

Correspondence connects a true statement with the actual state of affairs. Coherence evaluates how a claim fits consistently within a body of judgments. Pragmatic accounts emphasise the role of inquiry and practical consequences. The law of non-contradiction rules out a proposition and its negation both being true at the same time and in the same respect. Ad hominem targets the person instead of the argument. title: Traditional schools of philosophy and education
objective: Explain the chapter’s main ideas, distinguish its key terms, and apply them to an educational example.

blocks.text: Idealist approaches

The handout introduces idealism through an emphasis on mind or spirit and associates idealist education with intellectual and moral development. Plato’s cave depicts movement from ignorance toward understanding. Descartes’ cogito means I think, therefore I am. Berkeley is associated with the formula to be is to be perceived. These thinkers differ substantially; a chapter grouping does not make their systems identical.
Kant and an important terminology correction

Kant distinguishes objects as they appear under the conditions of our experience from things considered independently of those conditions. The appropriate introductory terms are phenomena and noumena, or phenomenal and noumenal. The handout’s word nominal in this comparison is a terminology error; it should not be learned as a synonym for noumenal.
Realist inquiry and faith and reason

Realism affirms a reality independent of our perceptions. The chapter associates Aristotle with form and matter, Aquinas with Aristotelian philosophy and Christian theology, Bacon with inductive inquiry from observations, Locke with the blank-slate image, and Whitehead with living ideas connected to experience. These comparisons help explain why educational approaches give different roles to observation, reasoning, practice and values.
Scholastic and Neo-Scholastic contexts

The handout connects the Scholastic tradition with Aquinas, reason and faith, and enduring truth and value. Medieval Aristotelian scholarship and the later Neo-Scholastic revival should not be collapsed into the same historical event: Neo-Scholasticism is a later revival of medieval Scholastic thought. Evaluate an educational approach by what it contributes to inquiry and formation, while examining its limitations rather than assuming its labels settle every question.

title: Java declarations, identifiers and evaluation

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

A Java variable declaration supplies a type and a valid identifier. int x = 5, y = 10; declares and initialises two integers; the paper’s int x, y = 5, 10; is malformed and cannot be executed literally. Assignment operators such as += and *= update the left operand; = assigns, while == compares and yields a boolean. The photographed CSC 232 quiz is Discrete Structures, matching the catalogue’s CSC 203 course. Of 50 students, 28 take CSC 232, 22 take CSC 201 and 12 take both. title: SDLC, software processes and products
objective: Apply the photographed paper’s concepts and independently check its examples.

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

Software engineering applies systematic engineering methods to developing and maintaining software. A process is an organised set of activities, while a product is an outcome of those activities. SDLC phases commonly include planning, requirements analysis, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. Project scope, estimates, risk assessment and a project plan guide planning. API and database design usually belong to design; implementing business logic and exception handling belongs to implementation; writing tests and evaluating results belongs to testing; installation and production setup belong to deployment; bug fixes and software updates belong to maintenance. Documentation supports several phases and is not exclusive to one. A software product is a software artefact supplied to users; a software service is a capability or activity delivered to a customer, often using software.

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

Symmetric cryptography uses a shared secret key; asymmetric cryptography uses a related public/private key pair. Hashing produces a digest and is not reversible encryption. Encryption supports confidentiality, while authentication verifies an asserted identity; they are different functions. Authentication factors include knowledge, possession and inherence, such as a passphrase, a hardware token and a fingerprint. Combining independent factor types gives stronger multi-factor authentication than repeating one type. Passive attacks observe communications; active attacks alter, inject or disrupt them. WEP is an obsolete wireless security scheme with serious weaknesses; WPA and WPA2 were later improvements, and WPA2 commonly uses AES-based CCMP. A man-in-the-middle adversary intercepts communications between parties; spoofing impersonates an identity.

title: Performance and the stored-program computer
objective: Apply the photographed paper’s concepts and independently check its examples.

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

For the same workload, performance is inversely related to execution time. If machine A finishes in 5 seconds and B in 6, A is faster by a factor of 6/5 = 1.2, or 20% greater performance. Equivalently A takes about 16.7% less time than B; those percentages use different denominators. A stored-program computer stores executable instructions in memory so the processor can fetch, decode and execute them. In the classic von Neumann model, instructions and data share the memory system. Integrated-circuit advances increase integration and can affect processor speed, power and cost. RAM is working storage with latency and capacity trade-offs; disks provide persistent storage with different latency and throughput characteristics.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: For a fixed program, performance(A)/performance(B) = time(B)/time(A) = 6/5 = 1.2. Do not divide 5 by 6 and call the result A’s speed advantage. Discuss hardware trends in terms of measurable latency, bandwidth, capacity, power and cost.

blocks.title: Read the source carefully
blocks.text: A 20% performance increase and a 20% time reduction are not the same numerical statement.
What to remember

items: For equal work, the ratio is 6/5 = 1.2.
The processor fetches stored instructions from memory.
Latency is elapsed delay associated with an operation.
The stored-program organisation keeps data and instructions in memory.

flashcards.back: 1.2 times B. For equal work, the ratio is 6/5 = 1.2.

title: CPU registers and bitwise operations
objective: Apply the photographed paper’s concepts and independently check its examples.

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

A program counter holds the location of the next instruction to fetch, subject to the architecture’s sequencing rules. An interrupt address register is architecture-specific and stores an interrupt-related address; exact roles should be tied to the machine’s stated design instead of assumed to be universal. For a bitwise expression A XOR B OR (A AND B), each operation is applied to corresponding bits. XOR produces 1 when the bits differ, AND when both are 1, and OR when at least one is 1. Therefore (A XOR B) OR (A AND B) equals A OR B for each bit. A generic assembly sequence loads the operands, calculates XOR and AND into temporaries, and ORs those temporary results. Specific instruction mnemonics depend on the chosen instruction set.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: For A = 1010₂ and B = 1100₂, XOR gives 0110₂, AND gives 1000₂, and ORing these gives 1110₂. Directly A OR B also gives 1110₂. Pseudocode: T1 ← A XOR B; T2 ← A AND B; RESULT ← T1 OR T2.

blocks.title: Read the source carefully
blocks.text: Do not present architecture-dependent pseudo-assembly as executable code for an unspecified processor.
What to remember

items: The program counter supports instruction sequencing.
XOR marks bit positions where the operands differ.
Only the leading bit is 1 in both operands.
The differing-bit and shared-1 cases together are exactly the OR cases.

title: Feasibility, fact-finding and information-system components
objective: Apply the photographed paper’s concepts and independently check its examples.

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

Systems analysis studies an organisation’s needs and processes before specifying a solution. A feasibility analysis identifies whether a proposal is technically possible, economically worthwhile, operationally acceptable, schedulable and legally appropriate; it also exposes risks and informs a proceed, revise or stop decision. Fact-finding methods include interviews, questionnaires, observation and examination of existing documents or records. Each method has strengths and limitations, so findings should be cross-checked. A common five-part information-system model includes hardware, software, data, people and procedures. Networks may be discussed separately in other models; state the model when listing components.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: To investigate a hostel ordering process, interview staff, survey students, observe order handling and inspect order records. Compare the findings before deciding the requirements. Hardware runs the system, software implements behaviour, data records orders, people use and support it, and procedures govern its operation.

blocks.title: Read the source carefully
blocks.text: Do not confuse a feasibility objective with a fact-finding method. Different textbooks group information-system components differently.
What to remember

items: Observation examines the process directly.
Questionnaires can collect comparable responses at scale.
This model includes technical, human and procedural components.
Feasibility weighs constraints and likely benefits before commitment.

title: Number representation, BCD and two’s complement
objective: Apply the photographed paper’s concepts and independently check its examples.

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

A positional number system uses a base, a digit set and place values. Binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal use bases 2, 8, 10 and 16. Convert to decimal by adding each digit times its place value; fractional binary positions use 1/2, 1/4 and so on. BCD encodes each decimal digit independently in four binary bits, so 347 is 0011 0100 0111, not the ordinary binary representation of 347. In signed magnitude the first bit is a sign and the remaining bits encode magnitude: 11001100₂ represents −76 in eight-bit signed magnitude. Fixed-width two’s complement is formed by inverting all bits and adding one, retaining that width.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: In eight bits, complement 11100111₂ by inverting to 00011000₂ and adding 1, obtaining 00011001₂. For 23.25₁₀, 23 = 16 + 4 + 2 + 1 gives 10111₂ and 0.25 gives .01₂, so the result is 10111.01₂. Also 85₁₀ = 1010101₂.

blocks.title: Read the source carefully
blocks.text: Keep the specified width for complements. Do not treat handwritten markings as the answer key, or decode BCD as one ordinary binary integer.
What to remember

items: Invert the bits to 00011000 and add one.
Encode 3, 4 and 7 separately as 0011, 0100 and 0111.
The sign bit is 1; magnitude 1001100₂ is 64 + 8 + 4 = 76.
23 is 10111₂ and one quarter is .01₂.

title: Boolean algebra, truth tables and simplification
objective: Apply the photographed paper’s concepts and independently check its examples.

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

Boolean algebra uses variables with values 0 or 1 and operations AND, OR and NOT. In Boolean notation juxtaposition denotes AND, + denotes OR, and a prime denotes NOT. Useful laws include identity, complement, absorption and De Morgan’s laws. De Morgan states NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B. For the paper’s expression ¬P ∧ (P → Q), substitute P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q and apply absorption, obtaining ¬P. A truth table should enumerate TT, TF, FT and FF. For F = A′B + BC + ABC, BC absorbs ABC, leaving A′B + BC = B(A′ + C).

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: For ¬P ∧ (P → Q): with P,Q = T,T the result is F; T,F gives F; F,T gives T; and F,F gives T. It therefore has exactly the same truth values as ¬P. For F = A′B + BC + ABC, first use BC + ABC = BC, then factor B.

blocks.title: Read the source carefully
blocks.text: Some photographed formula lines are too faint to read reliably. Only clearly identifiable expressions are used; no missing prime or symbol is guessed.
What to remember

items: De Morgan switches AND to OR and complements the operands.
Replace implication with ¬P ∨ Q, then use X ∧ (X ∨ Y) = X.
When BC is 1, OR with ABC adds no new true case.
At least one of a Boolean variable and its complement is 1.

title: Logic gates and integrated circuits
objective: Apply the photographed paper’s concepts and independently check its examples.

blocks.text: Understand the ideas

Logic gates implement Boolean operations in digital circuits. The basic AND, OR and NOT gates correspond to conjunction, disjunction and inversion. For two inputs, AND outputs 1 only for 11; OR outputs 0 only for 00; NOT reverses its single input. Digital integrated circuits implement discrete logic functions; analogue integrated circuits process continuous signals, with an operational amplifier being a familiar example. A conjunction can be represented as A ∧ B or AB. To verify a Boolean identity, compare the output of its two sides for every input assignment, rather than testing only one convenient case.

blocks.title: Work through an example
blocks.text: An AND gate with inputs 1 and 0 outputs 0; an OR gate with the same inputs outputs 1. To verify De Morgan for two inputs, build all four input rows and compare NOT(A AND B) with NOT A OR NOT B; the outputs agree on every row.

blocks.title: Read the source carefully
blocks.text: One matching input row does not prove an identity. Do not confuse Boolean OR (+) with ordinary integer addition.
What to remember

items: AND implements Boolean conjunction.
NOT is Boolean inversion.
An operational amplifier processes continuously varying signal values.
The expressions must agree for every possible input combination.
